newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss-Belgian balloon team plan weekend take-off.
newsitem.headline: Swiss-Belgian balloon team plan weekend take-off.

text.p: A Swiss-Belgian team of balloonists said on Friday that this weekend they would set out to fly around the world, a feat which this week escaped tycoon Richard Branson who crashed in the Algerian desert.
Bertrand Piccard, a Swiss psychiatrist, and Belgian pilot Wim Verstraeten hope to achieve a non-stop world premiere in a revolutionary baloon.
If meteorological conditions are right, the pioneering pair will lift off in their "Breitling Orbiter" late on Saturday from Chateau-d'Oex, near the chic resort of Gstaad in the Swiss Alps.
"It looks very good for a take-off this weekend, sometime between Saturday evening and Sunday morning," an enthusiastic Piccard told Reuters on Friday.

American millionaire Steve Fossett, who tried to be the first person to circumnavigate the globe non-stop in a hot-air balloon last January, crash landed in Canada. The stock trader from Chicago plans another flight soon from St. Louis, Missouri.
"The first one to take off doesn't have the most chance to succeed in this adventure. It is such a difficult experiment," Piccard told Reuters Television in an interview this week.
"Maybe the second or third one to start will have observed every possible problem the first one had and would maybe solve them before taking off," the 38-year-old Swiss added.
During their transatlantic balloon crossing in 1992, Piccard was able to hypnotise Verstraeten for brief periods.
They have been working for months to prepare their globe-circling flight from Chateau-d'Oex, which hosts an international balloon festival each January.

They hope winds will carry them eastward towards Greece, China, the Pacific, the United States and finally back to Europe, at altitudes of 10,000 metres (33,000 feet) during a roughly two-week period.
The sophisticated craft designed for their aeronautical exploit combines hot-air and helium-filled balloons, and is much smaller and lighter than Branson's model.
"I feel sorry for Richard," Piccard said on Wednesday.
"I have a great admiration for him, having organised such a fabulous expedition. To take off with such a tremendous balloon was already a success in my view," he said.

Flying aboard a pressurised capsule, fitted with the latest in navigational and communications gear, the Swiss-Belgian pair will rely on solar power and the helium balloon's lift during the day. A propane burner will heat the air and helium at night.
"We have no engine on board," Piccard said. "We plan to have the most simple material, but this material has never flown."
"If it works, it would be wonderful. But it is a prototype."
Piccard, who as a young man won the European aerobatic hang-gliding championships, works as a psychiatrist in Lausanne where he and his wife live with their three small children.
But he comes from a long line of adventurers.
His grandfather, Auguste Piccard, was famed for his inventions: the bathyscaph deep-sea diving apparatus, the stratospheric balloon and the pressurised cabin.
Auguste Piccard, who in 1931 became the first person to reach the stratosphere, was the model for Professor Tournesol in the Tintin cartoons of Belgian artist Herge (Georges Remi).
"Going to the stratosphere in 1931 was as fabulous as going to the moon in 1969," Bertrand Piccard said.
His own father, Jacques, designed the world's first tourist submarine built for underwater cruises and still holds the deep-diving record at 10,916 metres (35,815 feet).
"My goal is more an exploration of the inner world inside the human being. That is why I am a psychiatrist," Piccard said.
"We have to understand how the human being can use his life as an adventure," he added.
